name: East Route (Main Peak)
approach: Start at the Pete Lake Trailhead (aka Cooper Lake / Cooper River trailhead, ~2,800') at the end of Cooper Lake Road (FS-46); a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Follow the Cooper River Trail (Trail #1323) roughly 4 flat, forested miles to Pete Lake (~2,980'). Continue along the lakeshore and past its camps for about another 1.2 miles, staying left at the trail forks, to reach the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Turn north (right) on the PCT for approximately 1 mile as it climbs into the Lemah Creek drainage. Leave the maintained trail near the Lemah Creek crossing (the PCT footbridge here has been reported washed out in recent years) and head west/cross-country toward Upper Lemah Meadows — an intermittent climbers' path and sparse cairns mark the way for the first ~1,000 feet before fading into open terrain. From there it's another 1-2 miles of off-trail travel up the Lemah Creek valley — past small waterfalls and swimming holes, through several creek crossings, and some brushy slide-alder sections — gaining to a meadow camp around 3,600'. Most parties camp here or continue up the valley along the creek to about 5,000' where the glacier remnant/snowfinger terminates. From there climb to roughly 6,200' and exit left (south) up a short cliff step onto the glacial remnants/snowfields on the peak's southeast side. Traverse to just southwest of the main summit and climb a series of Class 2-3 cliff bands to the col between Lemah Two and the Main (East) Peak — this is the technical crux of the approach/climb and the point most trip reports flag for route-finding and loose rock. Total is roughly 16 miles round trip with ~4,700' of gain, and parties commonly take 8-10+ hours from trailhead to summit, so many split it into a two-day trip with a camp near 3,600'. Hazards: cold, sometimes thigh-deep early-season creek crossings on Lemah Creek; brush and downed timber off-trail; loose, exposed Class 2-3 scrambling in the cliff bands; and a genuine route-finding crux locating the correct gully/cliff-band line up to the col, especially in fog, low visibility, or lingering snow.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT, leaving the trail at the Lemah Creek footbridge
approach_variants.notes: Walk the Cooper River trail #1323 about four flat miles to Pete Lake, then roughly another mile and a quarter past the lake staying left at every fork to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn onto the PCT and follow it about a mile to Lemah Creek. The trail-leaving cue is sharp: leave the trail before the footbridge over Lemah Creek. There is a campsite at the bridge. If you have crossed the creek on a bridge you have gone past it. Note that it is unclear whether the Lemah junction is north or south along the PCT from Pete Lake, so navigate to the bridge itself rather than to a compass direction. A faint path climbs the creek side past waterfalls — Whinnimic Falls is the big one — and within about twenty minutes the ground opens onto rocky knobs. The valley floor above is flat and marshy at around 3,700 ft. Continue roughly a mile and more up the valley to the marshy basin under the long snow gully that starts on the north side of Lemah Five. Two lines lead from that basin up to the Lemah Glacier and neither is obvious from the marsh; one of them carries significant brush. Where the gully melts out at a waterfall, it is better to stay right and return to snow above than to scramble the left side. Leave the gully onto heather around 4,800 ft. One further note on names: Lemah has five summits and the main one is the middle, Lemah Three. Lemah Two is a different top on the same ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; the chute below the summit is easier as snow than as loose rock, so earlier is often better
hazards: Cold, sometimes thigh-deep creek crossings in the Lemah valley early season
Brush and blowdown on an unmaintained, lightly-used path
The moat beside the rock step
Loose rock on the final hundred feet if you take the gully rather than the ridge
Very poor rock quality generally — this ridge is chossy even by Cascade standards
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival is a rock step, called a chute in published descriptions, and it sits below the main summit after you have crossed the glacier basin and traversed north under Lemah Two.

The touchable sequence at the step, from a party who did it: pass a small waterfall, climb a wet gully for about ten feet, then work right onto dry rock. Those ten feet are the fourth-class move and the landing beneath them is relatively safe. That waterfall-then-wet-gully-then-step-right is the thing to look for; it is the crux of the whole climb and it is where the approach ends.

There is a tempting alternative that does not work: a ramp far to the left looks as though it would let you bypass the rock step entirely, but reaching it means an unpleasant moat crossing, and the party that looked at it came back down and took the step.

Above the step, the recorded mistake is worth more than the recorded route. Between Lemah Two and Lemah Three there is a small snowfield. A published sketch puts the line just left of the summit rocks, and following that into a mostly snow-filled gully leads to a difficult top, a snow bridge onto loose rock, and about a hundred feet of loose third and fourth class. The party who did that found on the way down that the honest instruction is simply: gain the ridge where it looks easiest. It is.

One route people have taken and should not repeat: descending a gully from Lemah One to reach the glacier. It melts out into very unstable talus blocks.

The Spectacle Lake approach is documented but has been explicitly superseded — the slide area between the lake outlet and the shoulder has grown into ten- to twelve-foot slide alder on a thirty-degree slope, dense enough that you cannot see over it to aim at anything.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the kiosk; Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required for the lot.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 80 (Roslyn/Salmon la Sac), go north on Bullfrog Road 2.8 miles through two roundabouts and continue on SR 903 through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake to Forest Road 46, about 16.8 miles from the freeway. Turn left (west) on FR 46 for 4.7 miles, then right on FR 4616 for about 1 mile to the Pete Lake trailhead at about 2,800 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass and a self-issued wilderness permit are required.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Established lakeshore campsites and reliable water on the east shore where Pete Lake Trail #1323 meets the lake.
waypoints.directions: Four flat, forested miles on the Cooper River Trail #1323 with barely 200 ft of gain — the easiest walking of the trip, and no measure of what follows it.

waypoints.name: Lemah Meadow / PCT junction campsite
waypoints.note: Small campsite marks the Pacific Crest Trail junction; leave the maintained trail here and head west toward Lemah Meadows and the peak.
waypoints.directions: Continue along the shore past the lake camps for roughly another mile, staying left at each trail fork, to where the Pacific Crest Trail comes in.

waypoints.name: Lemah Meadows creek ford
waypoints.note: Marshy meadow crossing forces a thigh-high ford of Lemah Creek's braids, followed by roughly 1,000 ft of slide-alder bushwhacking on the meadow's northwest side.
waypoints.directions: An intermittent climbers' path with sparse cairns leads the first thousand feet or so toward Upper Lemah Meadows before fading into open ground. There is no dependable bridge over Lemah Creek, so plan on wading rather than counting on one; the braids run cold and can be thigh-deep, and with high water this is a real obstacle rather than a nuisance.

waypoints.name: Point 3854 cairn line
waypoints.note: Trail fades into brush here; sparse cairns mark the cross-country line where Lemah's five distinct summits and Whinnimic Falls first come into view.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the alder the travel goes straight up the Lemah Creek valley — a mile or two of off-trail ground past small waterfalls and pools, with several more creek crossings and further brushy stretches. Expect wet feet for the rest of the day; there is no line through here that keeps them dry. Most parties camp on a bench in the meadows near 3,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Snow gully and moat transition
waypoints.note: Prominent snow gully gains the east flank; near its top, ~200 ft of wet slabs and running water lead to a moat where snow meets rock — tricky, exposed transition onto the ledges.
waypoints.directions: Carry on up the valley beside the creek to about 5,000 ft, where the snow finger and glacier remnant begin, then take the snow itself: 35-45 degree ground where crampons and an axe are essential and the runout below is bad. Crevasses are few but they are there, so a rope team is worth having across the remnant. Start early enough that the snow is still firm — this is the section that degrades to bare ice and open moats as the snowpack goes.

waypoints.name: Southeast ridge notch
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 ledges gain the notch on the southeast ridge above 7,200 ft; the final summit scramble begins here.
waypoints.directions: Cross the moat and climb the short cliff step onto the glacial remnants and snowfields on the peak's southeast side, then work across a series of cliff bands to the col between Lemah Two and the main peak. Finding the correct gully and cliff-band line up to the col is the route-finding crux, especially in fog or lingering snow, and the rock is loose.

waypoints.name: Lemah Mountain (Main Peak / Lemah Three)
waypoints.note: True summit of the five-tower Lemah massif, first climbed in 1923; last moves are exposed class 3-4 blocks on the summit tower.
waypoints.directions: From the col climb north toward the summit, then traverse west across the exposed ridge, going around or over a small summit block; the final 30 ft traverse west and climb the northwest ridge to the top. Gain the ridge where it looks easiest rather than following the snow-filled gully just left of the summit rocks, which tops out on loose third- and fourth-class ground.
